subtitle: Choosing a tense on purpose, and the German of 1517
words.intro: A monk may or may not have nailed a paper to a door in Wittenberg in 1517. What he did do is translate the Bible, in a few months in a castle, and fix what written German would sound like for centuries.

grammar[0].blocks[2].text: *Ich habe ihn gestern gesehen* is normal German. The choice is spoken (Perfekt) or written (Präteritum) — not finished or not.
grammar[0].blocks[3].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[0].fact: German has no *I was going* form. So tense can’t do what it does in English: *Ich las, als er kam* covers both *I read* and *I was reading*. German writers use *gerade*, *dabei sein zu* or *am Lesen sein* (in the Ruhr), or just let you work it out.

grammar[1].blocks[2].title: Where legend ends
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: In writing about history, Germans use *soll* and *angeblich* for legend, and *laut* for sources: *Luther soll die Thesen angeschlagen haben*. It’s the most honest sentence you can write about him.
grammar[1].fact: Luther’s translation did not create German out of nothing: he used the language of the Saxon chancery, because it was understood both north and south. But printing did the rest. The Bible sold in the hundreds of thousands, in a country where few could read, and where it was read aloud.

document.intro: A real title page of Luther’s New Testament, as pirated and printed in Basel in 1525. Spelling hadn’t been settled, as you’ll see. Say it aloud, and you can understand it. It even explains that hard foreign words have been put into German.
document.fact: Printers across the German lands reprinted Luther’s translation at once, without asking him. He complained bitterly. For readers in the south, this Basel printer added a list of his words they might not know.

reading.intro: A guide in Wittenberg, Frau Rösch, is taking a tour round the castle church. She tells the story the way guides do, sliding from one tense to another without anyone noticing. Max has had a German class that morning, and he has noticed. He has also started counting.
reading.photos[1].caption: Luther mit der Bibel, auf einem Gemälde. Den Hammer zeigt man hier nicht.
reading.fact: Luther translated the New Testament in eleven weeks in 1521–22, hiding on the Wartburg. He wanted a language ordinary people used: *dem Volk aufs Maul schauen*, to watch the people’s mouths. Whether he nailed the theses to a door is still debated. There’s no contemporary witness of it, and that doesn’t stop the replica door.
